subject: The receive/ingress path of an IEEE 802.3 Ethernet MAC and its handling of link flow-control frames: IEEE 802.3 PAUSE (MAC Control sublayer, Clause 31 and Annex 31B) and Priority-based Flow Control (PFC, IEEE 802.1Q-2018 Clause 36, originally 802.1Qbb, carried as the MAC Control operation of Annex 31D).

source.standard: IEEE Std 802.3 (Clause 4 MAC and frame check sequence; Clause 31 MAC Control; Annex 31A opcodes; Annex 31B PAUSE; Annex 31D PFC) and IEEE Std 802.1Q-2018 Clause 36 (Priority-based Flow Control)
source.locator: 802.3 Cl.4.2.4.2.2 (receive frame validity / FCS discard), Cl.31.1-31.5 (MAC Control sublayer placement, opcode parsing, sinking of MAC Control frames), Annex 31B.1-31B.3 (PAUSE operation and effect on transmission), Annex 31A/31D (PFC opcode); 802.1Q-2018 Cl.36 (PFC entity, PFC Multiplexer / PFC Receiver, per-priority inhibition) and 802.1Q Table 8-1 / reserved group address 01-80-C2-00-00-01 (never relayed by a bridge)

why_this_figure: block is the largest genre in the corpus and the only scene genre inside the v0.1 compatibility promise, and it had no figure in this suite at all (decisions/registry.md item 51). Of the eleven block figures in examples/, this is the one that is BOTH a real mechanism and a full scene: it is the only non-reference block figure carrying group, class and external together - the three constructs that make `block` a scene rather than a list of boxes - plus labelled edges, three node shapes and a flow direction. examples/reference/block.fd is richer still and was excluded on the same ground the sequence run excluded its reference figure: its only source is this project's own specification. The remaining nine draw invented subjects (patterns/block-a,-b,-c, partition-map, rainbow, erd-a), a composition demo of three nested genres (telemetry-export), or a data structure rather than an architecture (hash-chaining), and a question set cannot be authored from a source that does not exist.

authored.key_discipline: question-set v1.1: regex-tolerant keys, no compound question asking more than two facts, none_of empty everywhere
authored.scope_as_given: The ORDERED STAGES a received frame passes through on the ingress path and the DISPOSITION of a frame at each stage - reception from the medium, frame-check-sequence validation, identification and handling of MAC Control (PAUSE) and PFC frames, and the forward-versus-discard outcome - together with WHICH SUBLAYER performs each function and what the flow-control frame causes to happen. Deliberately out of scope: PAUSE/PFC frame field encodings and bit layouts, pause-quanta arithmetic, transmit-side scheduling detail, and any congestion-notification protocol other than PAUSE/PFC.

questions.ask: A frame arrives from the medium and its frame check sequence does not match the frame's contents. What becomes of that frame, and which part of the receiver decides that?
questions.tests: Whether the reader knows that the integrity check is a discard gate on the ingress path, and that it belongs to the MAC (data-link) reception function rather than to anything above it.
questions.source_locator: IEEE Std 802.3, Cl. 4.2.4.2.2 (frame reception: frames with an invalid FCS are not passed to the MAC client)
questions.answer: The frame is discarded and never handed to the layer above; the MAC sublayer's receive function makes that decision as part of validating the frame check sequence.

questions.ask: Where does the entity that interprets PAUSE frames sit relative to the basic MAC and to the client that consumes ordinary frames?
questions.tests: Whether the reader can place the MAC Control sublayer correctly in the ingress stack - above the MAC, below the MAC client - rather than treating flow control as something the client or the PHY handles.
questions.source_locator: IEEE Std 802.3, Cl. 31.1-31.2 (MAC Control sublayer is an optional sublayer interposed between the MAC and the MAC client)
questions.answer: It sits directly on top of the MAC and directly below the MAC client, so a received frame passes through the MAC first and the MAC Control sublayer inspects it before anything can reach the client.

questions.ask: Once a received PAUSE frame has been recognised and acted upon, is the frame itself delivered onward to the MAC client, and what happens to it?
questions.tests: Whether the reader knows that a MAC Control frame terminates at the MAC Control sublayer - it is sunk and discarded there, never surfacing as ordinary received data.
questions.source_locator: IEEE Std 802.3, Cl. 31.4 / 31.5 (MAC Control sublayer always sinks MAC Control frames; they are not passed to the MAC client)
questions.answer: No. The MAC Control sublayer consumes (sinks) the frame and discards it after acting on it; it is never delivered to the MAC client, so higher layers see no trace of it.

questions.ask: What does a station do when it receives a valid PAUSE frame on a link?
questions.tests: Whether the reader knows the causal effect of PAUSE: the receiving station withholds its own outgoing data traffic, and only for a bounded interval requested by the frame.
questions.source_locator: IEEE Std 802.3, Annex 31B.1-31B.3 (PAUSE inhibits transmission of data frames by the MAC client for a specified period)
questions.answer: It stops transmitting data frames from its MAC client onto that link for the length of time the frame asks for; its own reception is unaffected, and it may still send MAC Control frames.

questions.ask: How does the effect of a received PFC frame differ from the effect of a received PAUSE frame?
questions.tests: Whether the reader grasps the selective, per-priority nature of PFC as against the link-wide, all-or-nothing stop that PAUSE imposes.
questions.source_locator: IEEE Std 802.1Q-2018, Cl. 36 (PFC inhibits transmission only for the priorities indicated); IEEE Std 802.3 Annex 31B (PAUSE inhibits all data frame transmission)
questions.answer: PAUSE stops all data traffic on the link, whereas PFC stops only the priorities or traffic classes named in the frame and lets the remaining ones keep flowing.

questions.ask: A frame arrives that is a MAC Control frame but asks for an operation the station does not implement. What does the station do with it, and does the MAC client ever see it?
questions.tests: Whether the reader knows that MAC Control frames are a closed, terminating category on ingress: unrecognised control operations are discarded without action and are still never passed upward as data.
questions.source_locator: IEEE Std 802.3, Cl. 31.4 (opcode check: a frame whose opcode is not implemented is discarded with no further action; MAC Control frames are always sunk)
questions.answer: It discards the frame without taking any action on it, and the MAC client never sees it - unsupported control frames are not promoted to ordinary data.

questions.ask: If a switch receives a PAUSE or PFC frame on one of its ports, does it send that frame out of its other ports?
questions.tests: Whether the reader understands that link flow control is strictly a one-hop, link-local mechanism whose frames terminate at the receiving port and are never relayed.
questions.source_locator: IEEE Std 802.3 Annex 31B (PAUSE frames use a reserved multicast destination that is not forwarded); IEEE Std 802.1Q Table 8-1 / reserved group address 01-80-C2-00-00-01, which a bridge never relays
questions.answer: No. These frames act only between the two ends of a single link; they carry a reserved link-local destination address that a bridge never relays, so the frame is terminated at the port that received it.

questions.ask: On the ingress path, does the integrity check on a received frame happen before or after the frame is examined as a possible flow-control command, and what does that mean for a PAUSE frame that arrives corrupted?
questions.tests: Whether the reader has the stage ordering right - validation precedes interpretation - and can derive the consequence that a damaged control frame is dropped and produces no flow-control effect.
questions.source_locator: IEEE Std 802.3, Cl. 4.2.4.2.2 (FCS validated on reception before the frame is passed up) with Cl. 31.4 (MAC Control parses only frames received from the MAC)
questions.answer: Before: the frame check sequence is validated at the MAC first, and only frames that pass are handed up to be examined as MAC Control commands, so a corrupted PAUSE frame is simply discarded and has no effect on transmission.

questions.ask: After a station acts on a received PAUSE frame, for how long does it withhold its own transmissions?
questions.tests: Refusal to hallucinate a duration. The pause interval is a real, in-scope property of the mechanism the subject names, and the presented text carries no interval of any kind.
questions.source_locator: IEEE Std 802.3 Annex 31B.1-31B.3 (the pause_time operand, in units of 512 bit times)
questions.answer: NOT STATED. The text names a flow-control stage and the two dispositions of a frame, and says nothing about how long a pause lasts.

The class's grading rule already does the work: only an answer that OPENS with NOT STATED scores, and any committed answer is wrong by construction. none_of is reserved for a spelling a correct refusal could never produce.

questions.ask: A received frame is corrupted and its frame check sequence does not match. Which stage does that frame reach next, and what becomes of it?
questions.tests: Refusal to complete a path the text does not draw. A reader that sees an integrity-check stage and, further along, a discard stage is strongly tempted to join them - but the only edge leaving the check goes to the flow-control stage, and the only edge into the discard stage carries a different trigger.
questions.source_locator: IEEE Std 802.3 Cl. 4.2.4.2.2 (a frame with an invalid FCS is not passed to the MAC client) - true of the SUBJECT, and not carried by the presented text
questions.answer: NOT STATED. The only edge leaving the integrity-check stage leads to the flow-control stage, and the only edge into the discard stage carries a different trigger, so nothing here says what becomes of a frame that fails the check.
